evals.name: rollout-plan-build
evals.prompt: I need a rollout plan for moving our SDR team's outbound sequences from Apollo to HubSpot Sequences. 6 SDRs, two team leads (Priya and Tom), RevOps is me (Sam). Leadership reviews it Thursday and they are picky: they always ask who owns what, what happens when something breaks, and why we didn't do it another way. My rough thinking: migrate templates week 1, run both tools in parallel week 2, cut over week 3, switch Apollo off week 4. Help me build the plan.
evals.expected_output: Does not write the full plan straight away. Frames the review, asks a short batch of concrete questions (owners, inputs, failure paths, what is fixed), starts a logic ledger in the user's words, and explains the loop (questions, ledger sign-off, draft, rehearsal).
expectations: Asks the user questions before writing a full plan, rather than delivering a complete week-by-week plan in the first response
Questions are batched (roughly four to six per message), concrete, and ask what is already decided, who else is involved, and what inputs or volumes are in flight, rather than being a generic list
Introduces a logic ledger or decision record where the user's reasoning will be captured and signed off by the user
Does not invent the reasoning for the user's choices (e.g. why parallel-run is one week) but asks for it or offers options with trade-offs
Uses plain language with no slogans or punch lines

evals.name: scrutinise-draft
evals.prompt:
Here's my draft onboarding process for new client accounts at our agency. Poke holes in it the way my leadership team would before I send it to them.

1. Sales hands the signed SOW to delivery.
2. Delivery lead assigns an account manager.
3. The AM sets up the client in HubSpot and creates a Slack channel.
4. Kickoff call within a week.
5. Weekly status email goes out automatically from HubSpot.
6. QBR every quarter.
evals.expected_output: A rehearsal-style set of reviewer questions grouped by category (language, reality, completeness, ownership, control, reasoning, improvement), each phrased as a reviewer would ask, with the weak points called gaps. Flags the automated external email as needing a person to approve. Does not silently rewrite the plan with invented reasoning; asks the user to answer.
expectations: Produces reviewer-style questions organised by the draft's steps and/or by category, with a group for what is missing entirely, rather than a rewritten plan
Flags that the automated weekly status email leaves the company without a person approving it
Asks who owns each step by name and who the backup is
Asks what happens on failure or unhappy paths (SOW incomplete, AM unavailable, client does not show for kickoff, client goes quiet)
Calls weak points gaps rather than problems or failures
Asks the user to answer the questions rather than inventing answers on their behalf

evals.name: just-write-it
evals.prompt: just write me the 30-60-90 day onboarding plan for a new inside sales rep joining the HireRight account, I don't have time for back and forth, I need to send it to the account director tonight
evals.expected_output: Acknowledges the time pressure, states the risk in one sentence, offers the compressed version (three questions per block) and still produces a ledger with the user's decisions marked as open. Where it must propose, it gives options with trade-offs and asks the user to pick and give a reason, rather than silently deciding. Marks assumptions and 'to confirm' items.
expectations: Acknowledges the time pressure and offers a compressed path rather than refusing or ignoring it

Provides a draft now (does not make the draft conditional on answering questions) with the key choices visibly tagged as options with one-line trade-offs or as assumptions, and asks the user to pick with a reason
Includes a logic ledger or decision list with open rows for the user to sign off, one per tagged choice or assumption, with a short checklist for the user
Marks unknown facts as assumptions or to confirm rather than inventing them
Keeps language plain, with no slogans or punch lines

evals.name: perspective-coverage
evals.prompt:
Scrutinise this before it goes to our leadership team on Monday. It is our plan for running LinkedIn outreach for three clients through an agency team.

- Ops build the target list in Apollo and load it into the outreach tool.
- The tool sends connection requests and a three-message sequence from each team member's own LinkedIn account.
- Replies are answered by the team member who owns the account.
- When a prospect agrees to a meeting, the team member emails the client's account executive with the details.
- The team lead sends the client a results summary every month.

The three clients are in the UK and Germany. One of the team members is a contractor.
evals.expected_output: Reviewer questions grouped by the draft's own steps and tagged with category and lens, that visibly run more than the author's own view: the client lens (what lands in the AE's inbox, who approved it, response standard), the compliance lens (personal data basis for UK and German prospects, opt-out handling, LinkedIn's terms on automation and who accepts that risk, no invented sender identities), the continuity lens (history in each member's own account; what happens when one leaves; backup), the third-party lens (the contractor's employer, whose account they use, what the contract says about data and accounts), the finance lens (tool cost, price to client, baseline) and the measurement lens (what the monthly summary measures, against what baseline). Names the missing stakeholders (client-side marketing or feedback owner, legal reviewer). Calls weak points gaps. Does not rewrite the plan with invented reasoning; asks and offers options. Ends with a coverage line naming which lenses asked and which were left off and why.
expectations: Questions are grouped by the draft's five steps and each question carries a category letter (A to H) and the lens asking it, rather than one undifferentiated list

Covers at least five distinct lenses beyond the author's operational view, including the client or recipient, compliance or legal (data basis for UK and German prospects, opt-out, platform terms and who owns that risk), continuity (history in personal accounts, a leaver, a backup), third parties (the contractor's employer and account ownership) and measurement or finance
Names stakeholders missing from the draft, such as a client-side feedback owner and a legal reviewer, and asks who they are rather than inventing them
Calls weak points gaps, not problems or failures, and does not rewrite the plan with reasoning the user has not given
States which lenses were run and which were left off, with a reason, as a coverage summary
